observer-005.title: Separate a visible action from an explanation
observer-005.alt: The observation is that someone looked away before answering. Possible explanations include recalling a detail, feeling uncomfortable, and many others. None is confirmed by the gesture. A useful next step is a neutral question about the actual issue, such as which booking confirmation arrived, rather than an accusation about honesty.
observer-005.caption: Start at the single box on the left: that is the only thing you saw. Then follow the three arrows and notice that each one ends in a question mark. The gesture is the warning light; the three boxes are possible faults, and the arrows do not choose between them. Nothing here is a verdict about your friend. Fictional cafe scene.

cinema-001.title: Compare the saved doorway view
cinema-001.alt: Two matching doorway drawings retain the same shoes, laces, OUT card and door edge. Ghost door edges in the unsupported example indicate possible drift, not measured footage. Below, hands support a phone over a table.
cinema-001.caption: Find the phone first and follow the aim arrow to the shoes; then notice the card and the door edge, which are the three things you will inspect. Keep every position identical for both takes. This is a schematic layout, not a measured floor plan.

cinema-002.title: Fit the entire note delivery
cinema-002.alt: A true 16:9 frame contains a sideways folded-note delivery; a 9:16 frame contains a near-to-far route. A tall crop of the original wide view excludes the starting hand and landing square.
cinema-002.caption: Look at the two ends of the slide arrow first, the note and the landing square; both have to sit inside the recording. Then notice the phone stays put below them. A top view, not a measured layout.

cinema-003.title: Three views, three readable facts
cinema-003.alt: A wide view shows a teal bag by a doorway. A medium view shows a right hand opening its red pocket. A close view shows the same empty paper sleeve marked PASS, including its open mouth.
cinema-003.caption: Look at the three camera positions along the route first and read the question beside each one; then notice the bag never moves. These are separate takes at three zoom levels, not three cameras at once, and the distances are schematic.

cinema-004.title: Give rightward travel usable room
cinema-004.alt: Equal-sized paper arrows start at exactly one half and one third of equal frames. The drawn doorway stays near the right edge. Thirds guides divide each frame equally; the second start leaves a longer route ahead.
cinema-004.caption: Look at the open area to the right of the icon in each panel first; that gap is where the journey has to fit. The left-third start has parked with room on the side where the door will open. Positions are schematic frame percentages.

cinema-005.title: Paper brightness is not letter focus
cinema-005.alt: Four BUS 4 card views separate a brightness change from a focus change. A near dark sleeve enters without covering the card. The out-of-plane card is actually blurred with an SVG filter while the sleeve remains sharp.
cinema-005.caption: Follow the intended focus arrow from the phone to the card first, then notice the sleeve sitting between them, nearer the lens. The sleeve can steal the focus distance and darken the frame at the same time, which is two faults from one event. Top-view distances are schematic.

cinema-006.title: A larger BASIL label can be softer
cinema-006.alt: Far, middle and near trials show the same handwritten BASIL label increasing in size. Far and middle lettering is sharp; the largest near label is blurred with an SVG filter. A separate distance sketch shows the fixed phone and trial positions.
cinema-006.caption: Start at the far test and follow the arrow toward the camera; that is the order of the trials. The label appears three times to show three separate recordings, not three labels at once, and the spacing is schematic rather than a recommended distance.

cinema-007.title: White folds need distinct recorded tones
cinema-007.alt: The same towel outline contains a flat clipped white patch in one view and distinct ridges, creases and weave lines in another. A dimmed copy of the clipped patch remains featureless. A top view locates window, towel and alternative camera positions.
cinema-007.caption: Find the backlit camera at the bottom first and notice it is aiming straight through the towel at the window. Then find the light-side camera and follow its new view arrow: it faces the lit towel with the room behind. The two camera icons are separate takes.

cinema-008.title: Match the front house; compare the rear
cinema-008.alt: Pinhole-projected equal-height paper houses compare an original view, a digital crop and a nearer viewpoint. Actual rear-to-front drawing heights are one half, one half and one third. Camera positions at zero and twenty centimeters face houses at forty and eighty centimeters. A small fixed lateral offset keeps both houses visible.
cinema-008.caption: Read the two distances on the original camera first, 40 to the front house and 80 to the rear, then follow the move arrow and read the new pair, 20 and 60. The front distance halved while the rear only shrank by a quarter, which is the near tree looming. A schematic top view of the hypothetical setup.

cinema-009.title: Raise the view above the blocking wall
cinema-009.alt: A low view of a shallow box hides its folded message behind the front wall. A higher view reveals the same message inside. In a side elevation the lower sightline hits the wall, while the higher sightline clears it.
cinema-009.caption: Follow the blocked arrow from the lower camera first and notice it stops at the front wall, like a view stopped by a tall person in a crowd. Then follow the clear sightline from the higher camera over the wall to the message. This is a side elevation, not a floor plan, and the icon sizes are schematic.

cinema-010.title: Separate the post, plant and paper hill
cinema-010.alt: The same sharp foreground paper post, middle plant and folded background hill are initially aligned. A sideways camera change shifts the post most, the plant less and the hill least, revealing the plant outline without a blur effect.
cinema-010.caption: Follow the aligned view arrow from Phone A and notice that the post, the plant, and the hill all sit on it; from here the post can hide the plant. A top view in which the symbols do not depict actual screen sizes.

cinema-011.title: Steady hands still need safe frame margins
cinema-011.alt: Closed books and a paper marker appear in a full source view. A dashed inner crop excludes the marker. Two proportional saved-view examples compare that loss with a wider capture that retains the same marker. The crop amount is illustrative, not a phone specification.
cinema-011.caption: Follow the two arrows upward: the table supports the forearms, and the forearms steady the phone, like elbows on a fence under a pair of binoculars. The relationships are schematic; keep the phone in your hands rather than balancing it on a tall stack.

cinema-012.title: A slower pan makes smaller sample steps
cinema-012.alt: Triangle, square and circle mark a shelf pan from left to right. At the same illustrative 30 fps, four consecutive triangle views shift left twice as far in the four-second pan as in the eight-second pan. Sample displacement is enlarged for legibility, not drawn to the shelf overview scale. Counts are 120 and 240 movement frames, excluding one-second endpoint holds.
cinema-012.caption: Read the middle step first: it is the only part that changes between the two takes, four seconds and then eight. The holds at each end stay at one second so the comparison is about pan speed alone. Diagram spacing is not proportional to time.

cinema-013.title: The reminder changes where the book lands
cinema-013.alt: Four original tabletop storyboard panels follow a red book toward an open bag, discovery of a slip, the readable message LEAVE FOR JO, and the book left away from the bag. Suggested phases last one, two, two and two seconds.
cinema-013.caption: Read the first and last steps before the middle two: the book heads toward the bag, then ends up away from it. The two middle steps are the shutter on the shop, the reason for the turn. An original seven-second sketch with adjustable durations; the spacing is not a time scale.

cinema-014.title: Open a visible gap for the handoff
cinema-014.alt: Top views compare an aligned camera, nearer Giver and farther Receiver with the same camera facing separated stand-ins. Lower camera-view drawings show the aligned Giver concealing the note and the spread Giver on the left handing a note across a visible gap to Receiver on the right.
cinema-014.caption: Follow the obstructed view arrow from the camera and notice it has to pass through the Giver to reach the Receiver; the nearer body is the tall uncle in the group photo. A top view of the rehearsal layout, schematic rather than measured.

cinema-015.title: Map the cameras and the resulting eyelines
cinema-015.alt: Top view: A is left and B right on a horizontal conversation axis. The lower-left camera aims at B; the lower-right camera aims at A. Both are below the axis. The crossed camera is above it. Lower screen views show A looking right, B looking left, and a crossed shared view with B left and A right.
cinema-015.caption: Find the conversation axis arrow between A and B first; that is the net. The two cameras below it are the broadcast cameras staying on one side of the court. The single camera above has crossed the net, and from there A and B swap sides of the screen. A top view of alternative takes.

cinema-016.title: Give each plant shot an information job
cinema-016.alt: A wide table view separates a plant from its FOR JO label. A closer label view makes the recipient readable. A medium view shows the right hand returning the label to a visible position beside the plant. The three proposed durations total eight seconds.
cinema-016.caption: Follow the return label arrow from the loose label to its landing spot beside the plant, then check that the whole route is visible from the phone at the table end. The position is on the list for exactly this reason. A schematic table plan.

cinema-017.title: Both views need the same lift
cinema-017.alt: Two rows depict separate wider and closer performances of a right-handed empty plastic cup lift between the same paper marks. Selected moments show reach, shared mid-lift and placement. Cup sleeve dot, right hand and marks retain their orientation. Handles and all intervening phases are required in both takes.
cinema-017.caption: Find the Lift step in the middle first: that is the exchange zone where both takes must overlap. The still second at each end is the runner starting early and finishing late. Suggested 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 seconds makes eight per take; the spacing is not proportional.

cinema-018.title: Match the envelope at the same story moment
cinema-018.alt: Three states show a closed right-arrow envelope, a raised flap with the card hidden, and a partly visible HELLO card. A lower pair compares a correct raised-flap reset with an incorrect left arrow and prematurely visible card. Right hands are not mirrored.
cinema-018.caption: Read the three states as three positions of a board game in progress, and notice the right hand appears in every one; that is the detail that must not change between takes. Match the corresponding state across views, not every take's first frame. An original five-second sketch.

cinema-019.title: Same words, different playable invitations
cinema-019.alt: Both tabletop views use the line Have a look at this and the same original unfinished landscape sketch. In the welcome option the page is available; in the delay option a hand and pencil attend to its unfinished corner. A lower drawing shows a no-contact table placement rather than a compulsory handoff.
cinema-019.caption: Read the director's first line and notice it names a task, invite, not a feeling. Then watch the performer propose a different way to do it and the director keep the objective while dropping the contact. Original rehearsal dialogue, not a quotation from any actor or filmmaker.

cinema-020.title: Change only the open-card hold
cinema-020.alt: Two rows contain identical unfold, readable MEET AT SIX, and refold drawings. Below, proportional one-second-unit bars show take A lasting one plus one plus one seconds, and take B one plus three plus one seconds. Only the middle hold grows.
cinema-020.caption: Read the middle step first and notice it is the only one with two different numbers; the unfold and refold are identical in both takes. That is the saddle raised one notch with everything else left alone. Illustrative takes total three and five seconds, and the spacing shows order rather than duration.

cinema-021.title: Keep the look and pause; change the object
cinema-021.alt: Two three-panel sequences repeat identical original downward-right-looking and response faces. The first insert is a THANK YOU card on a low table; the second is a blank envelope from the same downward direction. A side elevation aligns drawn eyes and an insert camera above the low object. Neither sequence proves a real emotion.
cinema-021.caption: Follow the look arrow from the eyes down to the card, then the object view arrow from the insert camera to the same card, and notice they aim the same way from similar heights. That agreement is what lets the caption attach to the face. A schematic, not a measured reproduction of the character's exact viewpoint.

cinema-022.title: Hear the rustle before revealing its source
cinema-022.alt: A top-view table plan places an empty drawn square left and a paper parcel right. A phone turns in place from left to right. Three lower frames first show only the square, keep the same square during an offscreen rustle, then reveal the parcel. The sound cue is notation, not embedded audio.
cinema-022.caption: Follow the start view arrow to the empty square first and notice the parcel sits outside that view, just past the edge. Then follow the end view arrow. The phone turns from one fixed spot; the arrows show viewing directions, not a path for walking. A top view.

cinema-023.title: Recording yes does not mean posting yes
cinema-023.alt: Four illustrated panels show an agreed five-minute hands-only paper-folding recording, review by the two participants today, a separately declined public post, and tonight’s deletion plan for controlled copies. The same folded-paper image appears on each phone. Text warns that sound, reflections and backups need checking.
cinema-023.caption: Notice that the filmmaker asks two separate questions and gets two separate answers, like asking to borrow the book and then, separately, to copy it. The narrower answer is the one that stands. Original example dialogue; use it only after checking that the storage and deletion scope is something your device can honor.

cinema-024.title: Let the paper train leave; keep the figure still
cinema-024.alt: Three equal fixed-camera storyboard frames keep a paper figure and drawn platform in the same place while the same folded train moves right. A hand is openly visible during the slide. The final frame holds an increased gap, with all action remaining inside the tabletop.
cinema-024.caption: Follow the slide right arrow from where the train starts to where it ends, then notice the waiting figure has not moved; the growing distance between them is the whole shot. Magnets on a whiteboard, with every piece safely on a stable tabletop and nowhere near real transport. A top view of an original paper model.

cinema-025.title: Window fixed, camera position changes
cinema-025.alt: Three plans share a fixed window and subject position. The person turns toward phone A on the window side, B at the side, or C opposite the window. Corresponding portraits show two readable eyes, a nose shadow on the far cheek, and a backlit outline. Top: the person turns toward each phone position. Solid arrows show light; dashed arrows show the view. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-025.caption: Top view, not measured distances. Light travels from window to person; arrows marked view point from each camera toward the person.

cinema-026.title: Look at the shadow on the paper
cinema-026.alt: Two finger tests keep a similar finger-to-paper gap. A small apparent lamp produces an abrupt finger-shadow edge in this example. A broad indirect window produces a continuously graded boundary on the actual white receiving sheet. Both shadows have a dark core; softness is not global dimming. Keep the finger gap similar. Compare the edge width. Illustrative outcomes; not every lamp gives a hard edge. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-026.caption: Side view, not a scale drawing. Keep the finger-to-paper gap alike between recordings; the phone views the receiving surface.

cinema-027.title: Use white paper to return window light to a mug's darker side
cinema-027.alt: A top-view diagram places a window to the left, a mug in the center, white paper to the right, and a fixed phone below. Light travels from the window toward the mug and paper. Some light reflects from the paper back toward the mug's shadow side. Below, two simplified drawings show the same bright side and a lighter shadow side with paper. These are explanatory drawings, not photographs or measured results.
cinema-027.caption: Top view, simplified distances. The window-to-paper arrow clears the mug. Bounce travels from paper toward mug; the phone arrow means view, not illumination.

cinema-028.title: Intercept the wall light, not daylight
cinema-028.alt: Paired top views show an open white paperback, window at left, and pale wall at right. Without a flag, reflected light reaches the crease. With a matte dark cover between wall and book, the returning arrows stop at the cover. Lower drawings retain the same bright left page but deepen the crease. Top views: the main window-to-book path stays open. The dark cover stops returning light; it emits no darkness. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-028.caption: Top view. The returning-light arrow stops at the cover. There is no arrow sending darkness onward; the camera arrow only marks its view.

cinema-029.title: The lamp stays; the framing changes
cinema-029.alt: A wide drawing shows an intact desk lamp shining onto a notebook and a pencil held by a hand. The close drawing excludes the lamp but preserves the same left-to-right light and pencil shadow. A visible lamp and its useful illumination are separate things. Move the page into existing light, not toward the fitting. Close view: same light direction, lamp outside the frame. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-029.caption: Top view, not a clearance measurement. Light travels from lamp to page; two view arrows bracket the starting frame. A closer framing can exclude the lamp.

cinema-030.title: Move the phone, not the skin-tone goal
cinema-030.alt: Before: an indoor phone looks toward a person with a bright doorway behind their head. After: the phone moves beside the opening, still indoors, and the person turns toward daylight. The same person is drawn with clearer eyes and mouth against a quieter background, not a different skin identity. Both phone positions stay inside; keep the doorway clear. Compare expression and appearance, not a paler-skin target. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-030.caption: Top view. At A, daylight is behind the camera-facing person. At B, the person turns toward phone and daylight. Both camera positions stay safely inside.

cinema-031.title: One card under two different lights
cinema-031.alt: In A, a window and a warm lamp illuminate opposite sides of an actual drawn hand and white card. Both card and hand have a blue-to-amber cast. In B the optional lamp is off and daylight dominates both sides. An overall white-balance change cannot independently adjust the two regions. For B, switch the optional lamp off using its normal control. Compare both sides together; these are not calibrated colors. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-031.caption: Top view. Blue and amber identify the two sources schematically, not measured color values. Switch the optional lamp off for the second recording.

cinema-032.title: Check moving bands in saved playback
cinema-032.alt: Three successive schematic views of the same instruction card under a room lamp show a dark horizontal band at different heights. A second row, recorded in daylight with optional lamps off, has three stable cards. A single still cannot diagnose flicker; compare saved clips over time. These are schematic playback samples, not measured frames. Use supported timing tests or the daylight alternative. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-032.caption: Top view. A and B are separate recordings, not instructions to use both lights together. Keep card and camera geometry comparable.

cinema-033.title: Save the shoe position and its shadow
cinema-033.alt: A plan records the upper-left window, shoe toe pointing toward it, phone on the heel side, and table-edge landmark. A saved wider reference and a close knot drawing show the same lace shadows displaced toward the lower right. Restoring positions does not restore weather or guarantee matching color. In both views, lace shadows fall toward the lower right. Save the clip as well as the map; daylight can change. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-033.caption: Top view, schematic spacing. Restore these relationships, then compare the actual shadow and color in the saved clip. Weather is not encoded by the arrows.

cinema-034.title: Redesign the shot, not the wiring
cinema-034.alt: A top-view desk plan shows an intact lamp and an existing socket along the rear wall. Its cord stays behind the desk. The supported phone and notebook are on the desk, while a wide walking route to the exit stays clear. A separate daylight drawing is the alternative when equipment suitability is uncertain. The plan is not a clearance or electrical specification. If suitability is uncertain, stop and choose daylight. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-034.caption: Top view, not certified clearances. The wall arrow marks an existing cord route, not light. No cord crosses the foreground route to the exit.

cinema-035.title: Choose the take that reveals the note
cinema-035.alt: Three takes show an original MEET AFTER CLASS note over a coat pocket. A thumb covers the last word in A. B exposes the whole note. C exposes the note but schematic scraping noise masks required speech. The lower six-second B strip preserves reaching, unfolding, and an open-note pause instead of keeping only the reach. Choose B for the readable reveal and usable words. B times are invented. Keep A and C as alternative takes. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-035.caption: Invented source-clip times, not required performance timings or proportional widths. The reveal and pause are why B is selected.

cinema-036.title: Show the action that connects the views
cinema-036.alt: The incomplete order jumps from an empty hook above a bench to found headphones. The lower assembly adds the same bench with a hand lifting its scarf, connecting the absence to the headphones underneath. The corrected eight-second strip has two, three, and three seconds of picture with direct cuts. The scarf lift supplies the missing action and location. Invented 8 s assembly; red lines mark picture cuts. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-036.caption: A hypothetical eight-second assembly. Durations are examples, not a recommended pace or a proportional scale.

cinema-037.title: The cover should keep rising at the cut
cinema-037.alt: The first pair joins a halfway-open notebook to a closed notebook, restarting the action. The second pair joins the same halfway-wide pose to a slightly later close pose, both raised with the same hand in the same direction. Its output ranges are 0-2 and 2-4 seconds; the cut is instantaneous at 2 seconds. Compare the outgoing last pose with the incoming first pose. Invented timings. Check direction and speed during playback. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-037.caption: Hypothetical output times. The two-second boundary changes viewpoint, not the direction or starting state of the notebook action.

cinema-038.title: Forty source seconds, eight on screen
cinema-038.alt: A source ledger retains seconds 0-4 and 36-40 of an invented forty-second towel recording, omitting the middle thirty-two. The output strip joins one folded towel and two unfolded towels directly to a stack of three. With the camera fixed, the stack visibly jumps. Each timeline row has its own scale. 40 s source = 8 s kept + 32 s omitted. Row scales differ. The fixed-view stack jumps; the middle folds are omitted. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-038.caption: Source-time ledger for the invented recording, not proportional widths. Join the two KEEP sections directly; the middle section is absent from playback.

cinema-039.title: Count time after all words are visible
cinema-039.alt: Two timelines use the same horizontal time scale. Both take one second to lift a cover and two seconds to withdraw. A leaves USE SIDE DOOR fully exposed for one second and ends at four. B leaves it exposed for three seconds and ends at six. The uncovered interval is longer, not the whole performance. Only the fully readable hold changes. Both rows use one scale. A: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 s. B: 1 + 3 + 2 = 6 s; examples only. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-039.caption: Hypothetical six-second version B, not a reading-speed prescription. Only the middle interval holds the complete message still.

cinema-040.title: J-cut: hear the page before seeing it
cinema-040.alt: An eight-second picture row shows hallway A until output second four, then notebook B. The sound row switches to B at second three, giving a one-second lead. B picture uses source 1-5 seconds while B sound uses source 0-5. At output second four both reach B source second one, remaining synchronized afterward. Incoming B sound starts 1 s before its picture. Source ranges preserve sync; the sound marks are schematic. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-040.caption: Two timeline rows for the invented eight-second edit, not proportional blocks. At output 4 s, both B tracks are at source 1 s.

cinema-041.title: L-cut: the invitation finishes off screen
cinema-041.alt: A seven-second picture row shows the speaker for three seconds and an empty cushion for four. The original invitation remains continuous from zero to five, crossing the picture cut by two seconds. Compatible quiet room tone follows from five to seven. Words are not duplicated to create the overlap. From 3-5 s: outgoing voice, incoming cushion picture. Keep the sentence intact and synchronized before the cut. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-041.caption: Hypothetical seven-second timeline. The 3-5 s interval contains the outgoing voice and incoming picture together; rows are not a proportional scale.

cinema-042.title: Change only the neighboring image
cinema-042.alt: Version A is the same Saturday calendar, a brush tray, then the identical calendar. Version B replaces only the tray with a packed bag. Both have three two-second pictures and no music change. Painting or departure are possible readings, but brushes can mean cleanup and a bag can mean storage. Keep the calendar, 2 s holds, and sound alike in both versions. An association invites a reading; it does not prove an event. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-042.caption: Invented six-second order. A painting plan is one possible reading, not a fact established by these images.

cinema-043.title: Match first, then test a shared look
cinema-043.alt: A six-second check shows the same hand and marked white page as daylight A, warmer B, and corrected B for two seconds each. The corrected card and hand reduce the unwanted amber difference without changing their shapes or creases. Below, an optional restrained warm treatment is applied to both already matched shots. Compare the hand and page together, keeping detail visible. Page colors are illustrative, not calibrated skin-tone targets. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-043.caption: Invented comparison sequence, not a finished story or proportional timeline. Compare the same page and hand.

cinema-044.title: A flat picture does not identify log
cinema-044.alt: Three alternative picture tracks cover the same 0-3 source seconds, viewed one at a time. The original blue folder and a neutral saved copy retain separate crease lines and marks on the white page. An illustrative failed guessed conversion merges dark creases into the folder and light marks into the page. Compare one alternative at a time, not three stacked effects. Input format unknown? Leave unverified transforms off. All objects are original schematic drawings, not photographed frames. Colors and spacing are illustrative, not measurements.
cinema-044.caption: Compare one row at a time, not stacked effects. The failed result is hypothetical; it does not describe every transform or device.

design-001.title: Keep the pear. Change the field.
design-001.alt: Two identical, unoutlined pear silhouettes are #35654D. The left field is dark green #486754; the right field is pale ivory #F3EBDD. Neither the pear shape nor its color changes. The larger light-dark difference comes from the replacement field.
design-001.caption: Look at the pear chip against the middle chip first, then against the right chip. The pear is identical in both pairs; only the field moved. These screen colors illustrate separation, not calibrated paper or exact grayscale equivalents.

design-002.title: Name the change to the basil
design-002.alt: The same basil sprig and unchanged BASIL RECIPES heading accompany four adjacent screen-color chips. Initial #2F8F57 becomes muted #687A6E, darker #17482C, or blue #2F578F in separate candidates. These selections do not isolate perceptual properties mathematically.
design-002.caption: Read the label under each chip first, then compare that chip with the starting green on the left. Each chip tests one question: mute, darken, or change family. The values are not perceptually matched, and no slider is claimed to produce exactly these alternatives.

design-003.title: Same center, different surround
design-003.alt: Two 112 by 112 px centers have identical opaque #808080 fill. The left center is surrounded continuously by #202020; the right by #F2F2F2. Both surrounds measure 304 by 304 px. Compare apparent lightness while holding the target values and sizes fixed.
design-003.caption: Look at the gray center first, then let your eye take in the dark flanks on either side. The center is #808080 in both diagrams. Gaps separate the labels here; your paper experiment can use a continuous surround.

design-004.title: Which blue is warmer than which?
design-004.alt: An original railway-platform drawing uses violet-blue #5869A8 for its roof, green-blue #297E91 for the puddle, and amber #D79A45 for the hanging shelter lamp. Three adjacent chips repeat these exact colors. The roof blue is redder relative to the puddle blue; both are cool relative to the lamp.
design-004.caption: Look at the two blues first and decide which one leans redder. Then bring in the amber lamp and notice that both blues now sit on the cool side of it. These illustrative colors are not equal-value samples, measured lighting, or a calibrated painting reproduction.

design-005.title: Give each invitation color a job
design-005.alt: A seed-swap invitation has a #F5EBDD cream field. SEED SWAP, Saturday at 11, and Community room are all dark green #243F35. Three small terracotta #C55A30 seeds supply an optional accent. Covering those seeds does not remove any event information. Adjacent chips repeat the three role colors.
design-005.caption: Read the job under each chip first, then imagine covering the terracotta one. The chips show roles, not area percentages or approved text-contrast pairs. Nothing essential should depend on the motif color.

design-006.title: Light adds. Pigments absorb.
design-006.alt: Overlapping red, green and blue discs show full-channel additive combinations on black. Red plus green is #FFFF00; all three intersect at #FFFFFF. The key includes #FF0000, #00FF00, #0000FF, #FFFF00, #FFFFFF and zero-channel #000000. Below, irregular paint dabs show red #B44132 plus green #43694A and a possible muted #6A5542 outcome, not a paint recipe.
design-006.caption: Look at the three component chips first, then at the three results they add up to: red plus green gives yellow, and all three give white. These are idealized display codes. Black means a zero RGB code, not necessarily zero real display emission.

design-007.title: Change the view, not the map file
design-007.alt: The same original walking-map linework appears twice. Stored paper #E8E5DD and pencil #424242 are shown on the left. The right uses explanatory warm-view stand-ins #E8D4AC and #494236. The right-hand colors describe possible appearance, not a saved file edit or a measured display transformation.
design-007.caption: Look at each stored chip first, then at the warmer chip beside it, and remember that the file still contains the stored value. The warm chips are explanatory stand-ins, not a measured phone transform. The map values need not change when display warmth changes.

design-008.title: Keep a baseline before choosing a look
design-008.alt: Three copies of an original waiting-room timetable and bench retain the same drawing. The timetable patch changes from unwanted greenish #B6C8B7 to neutral baseline #C4C4C4, then to deliberate warm #D1C4AF. Neutral correction and creative warmth are separate decisions, with the baseline retained.
design-008.caption: Look at the middle chip first; that is the baseline the other two are judged against. The left chip is the accident, the right chip is the choice. These are illustrative timetable colors, not a tested transform.

design-009.title: A waveform keeps horizontal position
design-009.alt: Eight equal 80 px wide image blocks contain six dark #333333 blocks at the left and two bright #CCCCCC blocks at the right. Beneath, a schematic waveform stays low over the first six blocks and high over the last two. A separate horizontal histogram has bar lengths 336 and 112 px: six and two blocks, or 75 and 25 percent. Waveform heights are schematic, not an IRE or luminance conversion.
design-009.caption: Look at the two image regions along the top first, then follow each arrow down to its trace. Left stays left and right stays right; only the height changes, and that height is schematic signal level, not a measured swatch conversion.

design-010.title: Choose the light for your neutral
design-010.alt: An original room diagram separates a #AFCDE5 window lighting folded #C4C4C4 paper from an #E4B55F desk lamp lighting a #D6B47C amber wall. The folded paper has actual crease lines. Adjacent samples show paper before #B8C8BA, target #C4C4C4 and intentionally amber wall #D6B47C. Correcting the chosen paper sample does not require neutralizing the wall.
design-010.caption: Follow the left arrow first, from the window down to the paper; that is the light you balance for. Then follow the right arrow and notice it is a separate light with a separate target. The layout is schematic, not measured beam coverage.

design-011.title: A darker blank is still blank
design-011.alt: Two featureless rectangular source patches have identical geometry: #FFFFFF before and #BBBBBB after lowering the tone. Neither contains a fold. Below, two folded-program drawings keep identical crisp polygon boundaries. The soft pair is #666666 and #AAAAAA; the harder pair is #222222 and #DDDDDD. Tonal separation changes without changing edge sharpness.
design-011.caption: Look for a fold in the left patch, then in the right one. There is none in either, because the right patch is just the left patch turned down. This is a schematic case where the source has no differences left; it is not proof that every bright preview is unrecoverable.

design-012.title: Follow the paper across the cut
design-012.alt: An original vector wide view of a sewing table shows cream #C8C0AE pattern paper on blue cloth. Two larger views below retain the same pattern shape and cloth color. The close-view paper before is yellower #CFC3A4; the target repeats #C8C0AE. The close crops contain different paper-to-cloth proportions from the wide view. These are explanatory drawings, not sampled footage.
design-012.caption: Look at the middle chip against the left one first; that gap is the jump you see at the cut. The right chip shows where the close view needs to go. These are selected teaching colors, not sampled footage, and the identical reference and target codes simplify the diagram; real shot matching does not demand pixel equality.

design-013.title: Name the feature in the actual letter
design-013.alt: Large Arial h, e, o and g share a baseline at y = 338. A second dashed guide marks the approximate top of the Arial lowercase body. Callouts point to the h ascender, the open right side of e, the interior counter of o and the descender of g below the baseline. Hedge guide appears below at 56 and 28 px for a real-word inspection. Guides describe the system-font specimen, not every Latin typeface.
design-013.caption: Look at the e first and find its opening; that is the aperture that failed on the shelf. Then read the other three labels. This schematic uses the lesson display type, not a recommended font specimen.

design-014.title: Equal sizes, unequal lowercase bodies
design-014.alt: Two invented 16-unit design spaces are drawn at 12 SVG px per unit, hence 192 px high. Their baselines sit three units above the bottom. Original x glyphs have exact visible heights 84 and 108 px, representing 7 and 9 units. Below, Arial and Georgia render the same seed sentence at 36 px, without stretching. The named fonts are separate examples, not the sources of the invented metrics.
design-014.caption: Look at the two tall bars first and notice they are identical at 16: those are the frames. Then compare the two short bars, 7 and 9: those are the pictures inside. These are invented metrics, not real font measurements.

design-015.title: Read the recipe as a sequence
design-015.alt: The same exact directions appear twice in 30 px Arial: Rinse the beans. Drain them well. Add the tomato. The first is one running block wrapping after well. The second gives each complete action its own line with more space between actions. Wording and glyph size remain unchanged.
design-015.caption: Read the left version, look away for a moment, then try to find the second action. Now do the same with the right version. The words are identical; only the action boundaries moved. A short original extract, not a measured readability result.

design-016.title: Watch where the sentence wraps
design-016.alt: The same two sentences use 32 px Arial and 48 px baseline spacing in both trials: Walk past the old mill. Follow the path. In the 416 px column, each sentence occupies one line. In the 176 px column, the lines are Walk past; the old mill.; Follow the; path. Red return paths show movement back to the next left margin. Widths are construction dimensions, not recommendations.
design-016.caption: Follow the arrows: along the short first line, then back to the margin. Notice the return lands mid-sentence, with the old mill waiting on the next line. A schematic reading path, not a recommended width.

design-017.title: Move the baselines, not the font size
design-017.alt: Images: Héloise Ng, Sound: Hugo Gill, and Thanks: Jo occupy baselines 206, 266 and 326 SVG px. At the declared schematic scale of 5 SVG px per point, offsets are 0, 12 and 24 pt. A 10 pt body plus 2 pt added leading explains a 12 pt interval. Below, two real 32 px Arial credit blocks have 28 px and 48 px baseline spacing. Accents and g descenders remain present.
design-017.caption: Read the three names first, then the repeated 12 pt distance between their baselines. The gap is set like a shelf spacing, independent of how tall the letters are. This is an enlarged schematic, not actual-size typography.

design-018.title: Kerning changes a pair; tracking a run
design-018.alt: Three rows use the same individual 112 px Georgia A, V and A glyphs with explicitly centered positions. A coordinate unit equals 6 SVG px, with a fixed 60 px origin. Initial centers 20,50,80 give 30/30 separations. Pair-adjusted centers 20,44,74 give 24/30: both trailing letters move left 36 px. Tracking centers 14,50,86 give 36/36. These are center placements, not ink-gap or automatic kerning measurements.
design-018.caption: Look at the white space between the first A and the V, then between the V and the second A. The center separations are both 30 schematic units, yet the two gaps need not look the same.

design-019.title: Give the flyer shared edges
design-019.alt: A 600 px wide screening flyer uses 30 SVG px per squared-paper unit. From left to right its widths are 60,210,60,210,60 px: margins 2 units each, columns 7 units each and a 2-unit gutter, totaling 20. The title spans both columns. An original roof-and-window drawing and its caption start at x = 120; Saturday, 19:15, Library room and Book at desk start at x = 390. The shared edges are shown as vertical guides.
design-019.caption: Look down the left column first and notice the drawing and its caption share an edge; then do the same on the right with the details and booking line. The column centers at 27.5 and 72.5 percent are schematic; align actual content edges inside the margins and keep the gutter clear.

design-020.title: Keep each label nearer its own field
design-020.alt: Two fictional forms show Date with Sat 14 Nov and Venue with Library room. On the left, similar visible gaps leave Venue between fields. On the right, Date moves closer to its field and Venue closer to its own field, while the complete pairs are separated. A third sample wraps Venue and room name over two lines and keeps its field below the whole label. These are drawings, not live programmatic labels.
design-020.caption: Look at the gap between Date and Sat 14 Nov, then at the larger gap before Venue. The small gap makes a pair; the large gap separates the pairs. The centers are schematic, and real spacing must also account for text and control boundaries.

design-021.title: Let the entrance question come first
design-021.alt: An original Museum Night ticket gives GATE C the strongest type at 82 px and places it high on the ticket. Admission and 19:15 follow; Museum Night is smaller below. A numbered rail proposes gate, time, then event identity. The rail is an intended scanning order, not eye-tracking evidence.
design-021.caption: Read from the top: the gate first, then the time, then the event name. That is the visitor's order at the door, with the brand name moved off the front of the medicine box. Position records the ranking here; the finished ticket also needs its type size, weight, and contrast checked, and the reading order is a proposal, not a guarantee.

design-022.title: Give display, body and folio distinct jobs
design-022.alt: A chapbook page uses Georgia 64 px for Small Rain, Arial 32 px for The roof holds yesterday's rain., and Arial 24 px for folio 12. Callouts identify actual title, body and page number. Below, the same title appears in Arial bold and Georgia regular at 44 px, labeled sans serif and serif. These are real system-font specimens; only the title family changes in the proposed alternative.
design-022.caption: Read the three labels as three jobs first: introduce, keep reading, navigate quietly. Then ask which of them one family could do on its own. This is a spatial role plan, not a font specimen; compare real previews using these words before deciding the title needs a second family.

design-023.title: Read the date, not just the heading
design-023.alt: Two original repair-workshop samples use the exact same opaque #FFFFFF background. Both headings stay dark; the date Saturday 14 November and venue Library room change from #777777 to #595959 at the same enlarged display size. Their calculated opaque sRGB contrast ratios are approximately 4.478:1 and 7.005:1. The first is below the ordinary-text 4.5:1 threshold using the unrounded calculation. Sample enlargement does not redefine the large-text threshold or establish overall accessibility.
design-023.caption: Look at the first chip and read its ratio: about 4.478 to 1, just under the 4.5 line, like a 49.6 against a pass mark of 50. Then compare the darker chip at about 7.005 to 1. These are opaque sRGB examples on #FFFFFF, the displayed ratios are rounded for explanation rather than being pass decisions, and the chips say nothing about font size or weight.

design-024.title: Make room when the title grows
design-024.alt: A separate text-resize study shows the full title Saturday sketch walk for first-time visitors in two equally wide signup panels. At 32 px with 44 px line spacing it has three lines; at 40 px with 55 px spacing it has four. The 1.375 line-height ratio stays fixed. The last title baseline moves from 302 to 379, so Saturday at 10, Library steps, Join and the panel bottom all move down exactly 77 px. No word is removed and no later text is covered. This is a static reflow plan, not the distinct WCAG spacing-override test or a working signup control.
design-024.caption: Look at how much height the wrapped title takes first, then notice that the date and the Join button have moved down rather than being covered. This is the bigger lunchbox: schematic reflow where title growth pushes the content below it without clipping anything.

design-025.title: Review the date before confirming
design-025.alt: Three fictional booking components show Saturday with Change date, a selected Sunday, and Review change with Confirm and Cancel. Sunday is only proposed; no booking has been changed, and Cancel keeps Saturday.
design-025.caption: Read the three states left to right and notice that the last one is a review, not a confirmation. Sunday is proposed there; the booking has not changed. These are fictional interface states.

design-026.title: Name the two gallery actions
design-026.alt: An original Bent stem leaf drawing and a separate title sit above a View study link and a Keep offline button with distinct targets. Numbered focus stops put the outlined link first and the button second; this is a focus plan, not tested keyboard or storage behavior.
design-026.caption: Look at the two controls along the bottom first. One says where you will go and the other says what will change, and each has its own area to tap and its own focus stop. The card is shown without browser decoration.

design-027.title: A download is not an offline copy
design-027.alt: The same original park sketch appears in ready, downloading, interrupted-update and available-offline components. The pending state gives no percentage or duplicate action; Retry retains an older saved map, while Open saved map follows confirmed storage in this fictional example.
design-027.caption: Start at Download area and follow the arrow to Downloading, then notice that two arrows leave it. Only the Stored branch earns the Available offline label; the Failure branch keeps the old saved map and offers Retry. A fictional state diagram.

design-028.title: Repair the email. Keep the basket.
design-028.alt: The first fictional checkout retains two leaf prints, pickup name Lee and lee@ while adding the nearby error Add the part after @. The corrected review retains the same basket and name with the example address lee@example.test; no order is placed and deliverability is not asserted.
design-028.caption: Follow the three states and watch what stays constant: the basket and pickup name survive every step while only the email changes. The middle state is the circled sum with a note beside it. These are paper checkout states, not a payment flow.

design-029.title: Two menus, the same eight commands
design-029.alt: The flat alphabetical menu and the expanded File and Edit groups contain exactly the same eight commands, with Resize highlighted in both. File and Edit are shown open to expose their contents; the drawings predict no speed advantage and supply no measured search result.
design-029.caption: Find Resize in the left version, then find it in the right one and notice the extra step: you have to guess which heading holds it first. The commands are identical; only the search route differs. Neither layout has a predicted speed advantage here.

design-030.title: Contrast at the actual caption
design-030.alt: Identical captions use #777777 and #595959 on opaque #FFFFFF beside the same original leaf print. Their approximate ratios are 4.478:1 and 7.005:1; the unrounded values respectively fail and pass the ordinary-text AA threshold of 4.5:1, without establishing full WCAG conformance.
design-030.caption: Read the ratio under Caption A first and notice it sits just under the 4.5 mark, like a child at 119.5 beside a 120 sign. Then compare Caption B. Both are measured against the same white surface. These are specified opaque sRGB colors, and the ratios are approximate labels, not rounded pass decisions or calibrated screen samples.

design-031.title: Give each route a named status
design-031.alt: An original fictional map forks beside a pond: Riverside is dashed, crossed and labeled closed, while Garden is labeled open, with the same statuses repeated in a text list. Open does not assert safety or accessibility, and this invented drawing is not navigation advice.
design-031.caption: Start at the entrance, follow the arrow to the pond fork, and read the words on each route before you notice the colors. Then find the route list in the corner saying the same things in text. A fictional map, not navigation advice; the words should work even when all color is removed.

design-032.title: Keep the label, not the row height
design-032.alt: Both component drawings contain Email me about changes to this journey at the same enlarged lettering and available width. An actual SVG clip cuts the fixed row; the taller row shows the complete wrapped label and moves Reminder help down, without claiming a live 200 percent resize test.
design-032.caption: Read the label in the fixed row first and notice it stops at about; the rest is below the edge. Then read the growing row, where the table has been extended and every word is present beside its checkbox. A schematic comparison, not an enlarged screenshot or proof of a live resize test.

design-033.title: Measure targets, not icon strokes
design-033.alt: At four SVG units per stated CSS pixel, 20-by-20 targets with a 2-pixel gap have centers 22 apart and overlapping 24-diameter spacing circles; 32-by-32 targets with an 8-pixel gap have centers 40 apart and meet the basic size check. The Save and Remove artwork is unchanged; this scaled diagram is not a CSS-pixel ruler, comfort study or full assessment of the criterion and its exceptions.
design-033.caption: Read the center distance in each case first: 22 on the left, 40 on the right. On the left, two 12 pixel radii add to 24, more than 22, so the circles overlap. These are hypothetical aligned square targets in CSS pixels; the text describes the geometry and the illustration is not a pixel ruler.

design-034.title: Disclosure without hiding the result
design-034.alt: The same original basil seed-packet design appears with a checkerboard representing transparent surroundings and with the white surroundings of a JPEG copy. Filename, format, destination, conversion notice, unchanged-original summary and Save a copy remain visible while Image quality options is collapsed; no export is performed.
design-034.caption: Look at everything except the middle box first: filename, format with its white-background consequence, the note that the original is unchanged, and the action. That is the dashboard. The middle box is the only thing folded away, and its label says what is inside. Fictional export panel contents.

design-035.title: Prepare the staircase states
design-035.alt: Four prepared fictional components show an original staircase sketch in Gallery, Study detail, Kept for later and Saved items, including controls for opening and keeping it. These are author-prepared responses to possible actions, not participant instructions, observed behavior or evidence of successful usability testing.
design-035.caption: Read these four states as the examiner's map, prepared before the drive, not as directions to read aloud. Each one is what you show in response to an action the participant chooses, and only then.

design-036.title: Put pickup details before Continue
design-036.alt: Both fictional pickup panels use identical print artwork, quotation, Saturday date, 14:00-16:00 time and Continue label. The proposed panel moves the date-and-time group before Continue; whether readers find the time or expect a review rather than confirmation remains untested.
design-036.caption: Read the order of items in the current panel first and notice the action comes before the time. In the proposed version only that one relationship has moved, like changing a single step in a recipe. Fictional interface excerpts; the revision is a hypothesis to check, not a proven universal layout.

design-037.title: Build the bend before the outline
design-037.alt: Two original leaf studies contrast a rigid upright symbol with the lesson's drooping leaf. At left, attachment, blade, and tip keep rising. At right, the stem rises from a visible attachment, turns at a high bend, and connects to a blade hanging right. Red paths trace proposed gesture, not measured forces. The stretched outer curve and compressed inner curve belong to the same blade.
design-037.caption: Follow the arrows from attachment to tip and notice they never change direction. This is the leaf drawn from memory, the route with no turns. A simplified comparison drawing; the arrows trace the proposed gesture, not physical forces.

design-038.title: Connect the kettle's volumes
design-038.alt: An original tapered kettle is constructed from a rounded body, elliptical lid, loop handle, and tubular spout. The handle is behind the body and has two attachment points; one hidden join is dashed. A central axis passes through the lid and base, and curved cross-contours describe the belly. The spout has an elliptical opening and a direction continuing toward its attachment. Construction lines are scaffolding, not exact product dimensions.
design-038.caption: Find the body first and follow the Axis arrow up to the lid, which shares its orientation. Then follow the Attachment arrow to the spout and notice it comes out of the body rather than sitting beside it. Schematic volumes and attachments, not exact contours or ellipse proportions.

design-039.title: Check the space between utensils
design-039.alt: A wooden spoon and slotted spatula cross near the bottoms of their handles. Their inner edges bound a red wedge from an opening at the top to the crossing below. A separate narrow trial has the same opening height and crossing height but steeper boundaries. The dashed top of each wedge checks the opening; it is not another utensil. Compare boundary slopes rather than adding wood grain.
design-039.caption: Look at the Opening arrow across the top first; that width is the measurement. Then follow each side down to the crossing and notice those sides are the utensils' inner edges. A top-view checkpoint drawing; the upper connector measures the hole, it is not a third utensil.

design-040.title: Check the shoe's outer extent
design-040.alt: An original side-view shoe sits inside a five-checkpoint envelope: heel top, high opening, furthest toe, lowest sole, and heel base. A faint trial puts the toe too high; a short red arrow lowers it before lace detail. The lower study deliberately raises the ankle into a boot while retaining a shoe-like foot and sole. These are construction comparisons, not standard shoe proportions.
design-040.caption: Find the highest and the furthest-forward checkpoints first, Opening and Toe, because those two set the tilt of the whole box. Then follow the arrows round the polygon. An original envelope, not a shoe outline to trace; check its slopes against your own view.

design-041.title: Make parallel edges share a VP
design-041.alt: Two complete unbranded boxes demonstrate upright linear perspective. In the one-point view, front edges stay horizontal or vertical; three visible depth edges and their red extensions converge at the same marked vanishing point on the horizon. In the corner view, the two horizontal edge families converge at left and right vanishing points on one horizon. All vertical edges remain vertical. The horizons describe the observer's eye level, not a tabletop edge.
design-041.caption: Find the vanishing point at the top first, then follow both depth edges back to it like two car-park lines sharing one destination. The near and far widths stay horizontal because they run across the view. Projected plane only; the marked point sits on eye level.

design-042.title: Group light before texture
design-042.alt: Side light reaches a folded white napkin and brown cardboard. The facing napkin plane is light, the lit cardboard is middle value, and a continuous sheltered white fold is dark. The three colors follow the lesson's illustrative value plan, not material names or measured brightness. Below, the same little fold is drawn with uniform hatch texture and with a connected shadow group. Texture alone leaves the inward plane poorly separated.
design-042.caption: Follow the Light arrow to the facing plane first, then find the inward fold below it, which the light never reaches. The two napkin patches share a material and not an illumination, like the white car in the sun and the one under the bridge. A schematic arrangement.

design-043.title: Let the towel's edges differ
design-043.alt: An original partly rolled towel contains three different transitions. A light hem meets its darker overlap abruptly without an extra black border. The broad roll changes gradually from light to shade. Its loose tail fades to the exact gray of the backdrop, so part of the boundary is genuinely absent; a neighboring visible segment still explains the tail. Equal tail and backdrop values illustrate a lost edge, not a claim that every real towel has one.
design-043.caption: Find the three labeled places first: the hem overlap is the cliff, the rounded roll is the beach, and the loose tail against the backdrop is the marsh. Schematic towel parts, arranged so you can compare an overlap, a turning volume, and a boundary against a matching neighbor.

design-044.title: Two shadows, two surfaces
design-044.alt: An orange rests on a sheet of paper. The upper-left light corresponds to a bright upper-left fruit surface and a darker turning surface on the right. That form shadow stays on the orange. A separate connected cast shadow extends away toward lower right across the receiving paper, beginning at the contact. Red light arrows stop at the fruit. The drawing does not assert a shadow length, fixed darkness, or automatic bright reflected-light rim.
design-044.caption: Follow the Light arrow from the lamp to the orange first, then the Blocked path arrow from the orange to the shadow on the paper. The two arrows line up because the orange is the hill standing in the sun's way. An oblique setup schematic; the arrows show direction, not a measured shadow length.

design-045.title: Observe, recall, redesign the pouch
design-045.alt: An original zip pouch appears in three labeled studies. Observation shows a top opening on the top plane, a side plane, and an attached loop. The memory trial intentionally loses the thickness and misplaces the opening on the front. An invented version restores the volume and adds an upward-opening pocket attached to the right face. The pocket has its own top and side planes; red marks identify the structural change rather than decorative stitching.
design-045.caption: Look at where the top opening sits first: on the top plane, not across the front. Then find the side loop and the point where it attaches. A simplified front-view construction; study thickness from your own pouch rather than tracing these symbols.

design-046.title: Compare three boat arrangements
design-046.alt: Three original composition thumbnails contain a folded paper boat, a stone, and a broad cloth fold. The first places the boat low left and the stone high right along a diagonal fold. The second moves the boat centrally and crops the stone near the upper-right edge. The third leaves a larger quiet region by keeping the boat left, reducing the fold, and cropping most of the stone. These test placement and crop, not progressively more finished drawings or a universally best composition.
design-046.caption: Look at where the three masses sit before you think about what they are: low left, high right, and a fold running between them. This is one floor plan for the picture. Shapes stand for observed or invented forms, not a finished river illustration.

design-047.title: Study bands, matte tone, and folds
design-047.alt: Three original surface drawings share a steady light: a polished spoon with curved adjacent bright and dark reflected bands; unprinted matte paper with a broad, low-contrast tonal change; and folded cloth whose larger shadow shapes precede a little woven texture. Below, two bowl details keep the shape fixed while shifting a bright band for a separate viewpoint test. These are example reflection maps, not measured materials or permanent painted spoon markings.
design-047.caption: Notice first that one light reaches all three surfaces, then find the eye at the bottom, which is the only thing that moves during the reflection check. A setup map: objects and lamp stay fixed, the viewpoint shifts a little, like stepping beside a puddle.

design-048.title: Let the leaf lead the arrangement
design-048.alt: An original fallen leaf sits in front of a darker opening in folded unprinted cardboard. A single upper-left light is indicated. The leaf's pale blade has a clear boundary against that opening; larger cardboard planes remain middle value. A small lower-right pebble has a quiet edge rather than the strongest outline. Gesture, planes, negative space, value grouping, and selective edges support the stated intention to notice the leaf first, without claiming a guaranteed attention result.
design-048.caption: Find the leaf first and notice what sits directly behind it: the darker fold opening that makes it separate. Then see how the cardboard planes and pebble stay quieter, like props around the boots in a shop window. An original schematic and illustrative value plan, not finished artwork.

fg-017.title: Match the opening, not a habitual oval
fg-017.alt: Three circular-lid profiles have equal drawn major spans and exact minor-to-major ratios 48/60 = 0.8, 30/60 = 0.5, and 12/60 = 0.2. Their actual ellipse heights change in those proportions. Below, an enlarged 60 by 30 example shows perpendicular major and minor axes crossing at the center and four rim landmarks. Millimeters name the lesson's planned drawing spans, not physical screen measurements or conversions to viewing angles.
fg-017.caption: Find the two spans first. Left rim to right rim is 60 millimetres, the wide span. Top rim to bottom rim is 30, the narrow span, crossing the first at right angles through the centre. The ratio is 30 over 60, half open. Illustrative landmarks, not a traced ellipse or a scale drawing.

fg-018.title: Build tone with gaps and layers
fg-018.alt: Four original ballpoint-like patches contain actual strokes of equal width: spaced single hatching, closer single hatching, two crossing families, and denser crossing. The open paper gaps decrease rather than the pen stroke becoming heavier. Below, cross-contour strokes curve and change direction around a curled paper ribbon; a light section is left open. Coverage controls tone while direction describes a surface. The strokes are schematic, not calibrated ink or a required crossing angle.
fg-018.caption: Read the four swatches as four settings of the blinds, from open to nearly closed. Each step is reached by less paper showing, closer lines or another crossing layer, never by pressing harder. The tones are lightness targets only, not simulated ink; your paper and pen will land somewhere near them.

fg-019.title: Suggest ridges with cast shadows
fg-019.alt: Two original ridged-cardboard studies compare full ridge outlines with selected narrow cast-shadow shapes on the far side of the ridges. The second deliberately omits neighboring shadows. A lower cross-section explains the cause: parallel light arrows travel down and right, one stopping at a raised ridge and another at exposed paper to its left. A dark receiving patch is behind the ridge on the right. No light arrow continues into that blocked patch. Shadow length is illustrative, not measured.
fg-019.caption: Follow the two arrows from the light. One stops at the ridge: that is the blocking, and the dark patch at lower right sits in the gap the ridge creates. The other reaches the exposed paper at lower left with nothing in the way. No arrow enters the shaded patch, which is the whole point. Illustrative cross-section, not measured lighting.

fg-020.title: Scale the leaf, not just the frame
fg-020.alt: The same original curved leaf is drawn in a four-by-four grid inside a 4 cm square and an 8 cm square. The target is twice the source width and twice its height, not just a relabeled same-size grid. Source cells are 1 cm and target cells 2 cm. From each upper-left origin, tip (2, 0.5) becomes (4, 1), stem join (2, 3.5) becomes (4, 7), widest left (0.75, 2) becomes (1.5, 4), and widest right (3.25, 2) becomes (6.5, 4). All four landmarks retain their within-cell positions. Screen centimeters are not physically calibrated.
fg-020.caption: Find the four circles and read the centimetre labels: each target coordinate is exactly double its source, tip (2, 0.5) to (4, 1), widest left (0.75, 2) to (1.5, 4), and so on. The arrows only show the order you travel round the contour; the real leaf edge curves between these anchors, so draw those curves on paper from the original. Schematic positions, not to screen scale.
